design-nao-e-so-o-que-voce-ve.title: Design is not just what you see
design-nao-e-so-o-que-voce-ve.summary: Between aesthetics, strategy, and perception, a reflection on what truly makes a visual identity work.
design-nao-e-so-o-que-voce-ve.seo_title: Design beyond aesthetics: identity and perception
design-nao-e-so-o-que-voce-ve.seo_description: What transforms a visual identity into a brand experience? A reflection on art direction, strategy, and perception.
design-nao-e-so-o-que-voce-ve.body:
# Design is not just what you see

There's something curious about design: many people only notice it when something is wrong.

A typeface that doesn't fit. A color that seems out of place. A brand that tries to appear sophisticated, but fails to maintain that impression.

And sometimes, everything looks beautiful. It just doesn't communicate anything at all.

That's where the conversation gets interesting.

## Looking good doesn't mean it works

Aesthetics matter. Of course they do.

But it's a part of the job, not the whole job.

A visual identity needs to answer questions that go far beyond choosing a font or a color combination.

Who is this brand? What does it represent? Who is it speaking to? Why should anyone pay attention to it?

Without these answers, even the best visual composition risks becoming mere decoration.

## What exists before the first layout?

I like to think that a project begins long before you even open any software.

It starts with conversation, research, references, and, most importantly, asking the right questions.

Here are some points that I consider essential in this process:

* **Context:** understand the business, its market, and the people it interacts with.
* **Intention:** define what the communication needs to convey.
* **Consistency:** build a visual language that works across different applications.
* **Perception:** observe how visual choices influence how the brand is perceived.

None of this guarantees a perfect solution. But it helps us make decisions we can explain and defend.

## Identity is perception

A brand doesn't exist solely in the final file delivered to the client.

It's present in the packaging, the customer service, the website, the sales presentation, and even in the way it replies to a message.

Every interaction creates an impression.

> A visual identity doesn't need to say everything. It needs to communicate what really matters.

Therefore, art direction is also an exercise in choice. What to highlight, what to reduce, what to repeat and, above all, what to leave out.

## Fewer effects, more intention

Not every project needs elaborate animation, experimental typography, or a striking composition.

Sometimes, the best decision is precisely the most discreet one.

The challenge lies in understanding when each visual choice contributes to the message and when it exists solely to attract attention.

Ultimately, the job isn't to make everything seem interesting.

It's about making sure the right things are noticed.

***

*This is a demonstration article created to test the editorial system of Pausa do café.*

designers-em-tempos-de-ia-estamos-tercei.title: Designers in the age of AI: are we outsourcing even our thinking?
designers-em-tempos-de-ia-estamos-tercei.summary: AI is transforming design, but are we losing the habit of thinking for ourselves? A reflection on creativity, the undervaluing of design work, and the role of critical thinking in the future of the profession.
designers-em-tempos-de-ia-estamos-tercei.seo_title: Designers in the age of AI: the future of the profession
designers-em-tempos-de-ia-estamos-tercei.seo_description: How is artificial intelligence changing the work of designers? A reflection on creativity, the market, critical thinking, and the future of the profession.
designers-em-tempos-de-ia-estamos-tercei.body:
For the first post on this blog, I wanted to talk about something that has been keeping many of us in design awake at night: **the future of design in the age of artificial intelligence**. But before we talk about AI, let's remember that our problems didn't start with ChatGPT.

## Even before AI, things weren't easy

I'm from Fortaleza, in Ceará, and I've always had the impression that design has never received the recognition it deserves here. When I started in a print shop, it was common to find people who thought our work was easy; after all, we just sat in front of a computer. As if all it took was opening Photoshop, pressing a few buttons, and that's it: the artwork was done.

Then came the social media boom. Suddenly, in addition to being a designer, you had to be an influencer, produce content, sell courses, and build an audience. Within agencies, the demand only increased, while the space to explore ideas decreased. **Creative departments became production lines for carousels, posts, and stories.** It's not that this work doesn't require creativity, but when everything becomes urgent and focused on quantity, there's little time left to think. I know professionals who gave up on the field during that period. And, honestly, little has improved since then.

## And then came artificial intelligence

As if things weren't complicated enough, along came generative AI. First, the concern reached writers and journalists. Soon after, image generation placed designers and art directors at the center of the discussion. At first, the technology seemed like just another support tool: generate an image, refine it, and work it into a layout. But the change was rapid. **Today, we already see entire designs generated by AI, with designers stepping in only to make adjustments and prepare the final files.** In some companies, what was once a possibility has become a requirement.

The problem isn't using artificial intelligence. I myself recognize its potential. The issue is when productivity starts replacing the creative process and, worse, professional judgment itself.

## Are we outsourcing even our thinking?

I've seen managers and creative professionals asking AI to evaluate visual identities, logos, and graphic work. The tool points out possible improvements, and these recommendations reach the designer as changes to be made, often without any questioning. A second opinion is valid, but **when a machine's answer becomes absolute truth, we are outsourcing not only the execution but also our critical judgment.**

A visual identity doesn't appear out of thin air. Behind each project are research, a brief, strategy, a body of references, and a series of decisions. AI can analyze an image, but that doesn't mean it understands all the choices that led to that result. And when we have to justify our work in the face of an automated evaluation, without anyone questioning its criteria, something is amiss.

## What's left for the designer?

Alexandre Wollner, one of the pioneers of Brazilian design, argued that design is a process of planning and problem-solving, rather than just illustration or decoration. It's curious to think about that now, when we can generate dozens of visual alternatives in seconds. **If design involves planning and problem-solving, it cannot be reduced to the final image.**

I don't believe we should fight against AI. The technology is here to stay, and we need to learn how to work with it. But perhaps the greatest challenge of our profession isn't mastering the next tool or writing better prompts. Perhaps it's something more important: **holding on to our ability to think, question, and create with intention.**

Because, ultimately, if we start outsourcing our critical thinking as well, **what exactly will be left of our work?**

o-futuro-da-criatividade-comeca-com-uma-.title: The future of creativity begins with a pause

o-futuro-da-criatividade-comeca-com-uma-.seo_title: Creativity and references: the importance of taking breaks
o-futuro-da-criatividade-comeca-com-uma-.seo_description: Creating also requires observation, research, and reflection. Understand why taking breaks can contribute to more conscious creative decisions.
o-futuro-da-criatividade-comeca-com-uma-.body:
# The future of creativity begins with a pause

We spend a good part of the day producing. Creating layouts, searching for references, solving problems, and trying to find the next good idea.

But there's a question we rarely ask ourselves: are we dedicating enough time to thinking?

## Creating is not just producing

The creative industry constantly demands speed. We need to deliver more, adapt more, and learn more.

But creativity doesn't depend exclusively on how much we produce.

It also depends on what we observe, study, and are able to connect.

## Building a body of references

A good idea can be born from a conversation, a book, an exhibition, or something seemingly unrelated to design.

The more references we have, the more possibilities we can see.

Building that body of references is also part of an art director's job.

> Not every pause is an interruption. Some are an essential part of the creative process.

## What do we take from this?

Perhaps the challenge isn't finding ways to produce more and more.

Perhaps it's about learning to produce with more intention.

Creating requires technical skill, sensitivity, research, and time to transform information into something relevant.

And sometimes, it all starts with a pause.

***

*This is a demonstration article for validating the scheduled publication system of Pausa do café.*
